source: Antony, Ferreira, Norman, Wimber (2017) Retrieval as a fast route to memory consolidation
finding: Founding proposal for this subfield. Retrieval is a rapid, online consolidation event. Retrieval re-activates a memory through pattern completion and co-activates linked neocortical knowledge. This integrates the memory into neocortex and differentiates it from competitors, so it becomes less hippocampus-dependent. Restudy re-imposes the whole original pattern and co-activates less, so it does not do this.
numbers: No new data. Four-page TICS Forum piece with one figure and a Box of predictions: vmPFC up and hippocampus down for retrieved vs restudied items; retrieval benefit should shrink for novel material without neocortical schemas.
quote: retrieval acts as a rapid consolidation event, supporting the creation of adaptive hippocampal-neocortical representations via the online reactivation of associative information
limits: Theory and a synthesis, not a test. Rests on CLS and on a few behavioural parallels (sleep, interference, fast mapping). Authors admit sleep has unique features and it is unclear if sleep reactivation is as imprecise as wake retrieval.
agent_relevance: Background framing: remembering a lesson is itself a write operation, not only a read. For our scaffold this suggests re-deriving a lesson from a cue (not re-reading it) is what stabilises it. Only an analogy for an agent without weights.

source: Antony et al. (2017) - mechanism: integration vs differentiation by co-activation strength
finding: Mechanistic core taken from Norman's non-monotonic plasticity idea: strong co-activation of related memories leads to integration; moderate co-activation of competitors leads to weakening and representational push-apart. Both follow because retrieval is imprecise and co-activates neighbours.
numbers: Worked example in Fig 1: a new taxi-phone episode and an older taxi-suitcase episode share the node taxi in neocortex; retrieval of one co-activates the other.
limits: Qualitative; no parameters fitted in this paper. Quantitative version lives in Norman et al. 2007 (see later line).
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for a lesson store: retrieving one lesson with a cue that partly matches a neighbour either merges them or separates them depending on how strongly the neighbour fires. Worth noting for cue-overload design.

source: Antony et al. (2017) - behavioural parallels to sleep consolidation
finding: Four parallels offered. (1) Testing effects grow with delay (days to weeks). (2) Both sleep and retrieval protect against retroactive interference (Potts and Shanks 2012 for retrieval). (3) Restudied items gain more from sleep than retrieved items (Bauml 2014). (4) Fast-mapping and schema-consistent learning also skip the need for sleep.
numbers: Cites Rowland 2014 meta-analysis, Bauml 2014, Himmer 2016 fast mapping, Sharon 2011 amnesic patients, Tse 2007, Wing 2013.
limits: Parallel 3 has a competing explanation: the bifurcation model (Kornell, Bjork, Garcia 2011) says retrieved items are simply already above threshold. The same data fit both.
agent_relevance: Reminds us the consolidation story is one of several accounts; do not hard-code it into the schema.

source: Himmer, Schonauer, Heib, Schabus, Gais (2019) Rehearsal initiates systems memory consolidation, sleep makes it last
finding: Seven learn-then-free-recall rounds of one 28-word list shifted activity within one session: hippocampus and mPFC fell, precuneus and inferior parietal lobule rose. This is a fast systems-consolidation-like transition. Sleep (not wake) kept the hippocampus disengaged for old words 12 h later.
numbers: N = 31 (wake 16, sleep 15). 28 German nouns, 7 encode-recall rounds. Linear decline in hippocampus beta = 0.864, R2 = 0.748; mPFC 0.839; precuneus rise 0.913, R2 = 0.834; IPL 0.952, R2 = 0.907. Three-way interaction (sleep/wake x old/new x first/last) in left hippocampus F(1,29) = 6.68, P = 0.015. Old words in sleep group: slope not different from 0 (t14 = 0.20); in wake group declined (t15 = 2.51, P = 0.024).
quote: repeated study induces systems consolidation, while sleep ensures that these transformations become stable and long lasting
limits: Rehearsal here is study plus free recall, so retrieval is confounded with re-exposure; no restudy control. Small groups. Effect of sleep on precuneus not significant. Authors note the alternative of parallel hippocampal and neocortical encoding.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that repeated recall quickly moves a trace toward a more durable store, but also that something slower (sleep) is needed to make it stick. For an agent: an immediate recall pass helps, but a later re-check may still be needed.

source: Ferreira, Charest, Wimber (2018 preprint) Testing the fast consolidation hypothesis of retrieval-mediated learning
finding: First direct test of Antony et al. Retrieval-specific mPFC activation rose within session 1, as predicted. But hippocampal activation did not fall within a session; it fell only across the two days. Semantic coding in parietal cortex also appeared only across days. So the data fit a mix of fast and slow change.
numbers: N = 22 analysed (24 tested; 2 excluded). 128 scenes and 128 objects in 8 semantic categories; 4 practice cycles over 2 sessions 2 days apart. mPFC retrieval slope t(19) = 3.66, p = .001; restudy slope t(19) = -0.65; slope difference t(19) = 2.60, p = .009. Hippocampus within-session slope difference t(19) = 1.69, p = .107 (n.s.). Retrieval hippocampal drop day 1 to day 2 t(19) = 2.02, p = .029, but condition x cycle F(1,19) = 3.48, p = .078. Practice accuracy: restudy .89 vs retrieval .79.
limits: Preprint, small N, uncorrected p < .001 thresholds in whole-brain work, marginal interaction on the key hippocampal test. No final behavioural test result found in the text read. Peer-reviewed version may differ.
agent_relevance: Warns that the fast version of the story is only partly supported; the slow version (needs time) is better supported. Do not assume one retrieval pass fully consolidates.

source: Ferreira et al. (2018) - what was predicted
finding: Three predictions derived from the framework: (1) mPFC up and hippocampus down across retrievals; (2) gist-like items, so same-category items grow more similar across retrievals; (3) episode-unique information is also strengthened (retrieval reduces overlap between similar memories). Timescale was the key unknown: within session means fast online, across days means interaction with offline consolidation.
numbers: Prediction 2 not found within session; found across sessions in precuneus, cingulate, left superior temporal and supramarginal gyrus.
limits: Evidence on whether gist formation costs contextual detail is mixed in the systems consolidation literature (Cairney 2011 vs Jurewicz 2016, as cited there).
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist of observable signatures; useful when judging any later claim that retrieval consolidates.

source: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention
finding: Experiment 1: one study plus a free-recall test beats two study periods at 2 days and 1 week, but loses at 5 min. This crossover is the classic testing effect. Founding behavioural result for the whole subfield.
numbers: Prose passages, 30 idea units. 5 min: restudy 81% vs test 75%, d = 0.52. 2 days: test 68% vs restudy 54%, d = 0.95. 1 week: test 56% vs restudy 42%, d = 0.83. Interaction F(2,117) = 32.10, partial eta2 = .35. Initial test recall about 70% (20.9 of 30 units). Tested group at 1 week matched restudy group at 2 days.
limits: No feedback, free recall of prose, tests between 5 min and 1 week only.
agent_relevance: Establishes the behavioural fact the consolidation story tries to explain. Cost note: retrieval looks worse at short delays; a scaffold judged only on immediate output would wrongly prefer re-reading.

source: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) - Experiment 2 and confidence
finding: Experiment 2 compared SSSS (study 4x), SSST, STTT (study once, test 3x). Passage readings were 14.2, 10.3 and 3.4. Subjects in the repeated-study group were the most confident of remembering in a week.
numbers: Confidence SSSS higher than SSST t(118) = 2.95, d = 0.54, and than STTT t(118) = 3.35, d = 0.61. Mean rating of expected recall 4.8 (SSSS), 4.2 (SSST), 4.0 (STTT) on a 7-point scale. STTT initial tests recalled 20.9, 21.2, 21.1 idea units.
limits: Delayed-test outcome numbers for Exp 2 were not extracted in this session; only the process and confidence data are recorded here.
agent_relevance: Illusion of competence: more re-reading feels better and works worse. A self-judged 'I have this' is not a reliable signal.

source: Karpicke and Roediger (2008) The critical importance of retrieval for learning
finding: Dropout design on 40 Swahili-English pairs. Once a pair was recalled once, it was dropped from study, from test, from both, or kept. Dropping from further study did nothing a week later. Dropping from further testing cut recall by more than half. So retrieval, not re-exposure, carried the learning after first success.
numbers: Final recall at 1 week: ST and SNT (repeated testing) about 80%; STN 36% and SNTN 33% (dropped from testing). Combined effect of repeated retrieval d = 4.03; repeated-test range 63-95%, dropout range 10-60% with no overlap. Predicted recall about 50% in all four conditions (means 20.8, 20.4, 22.0, 20.3 of 40). Trials: 320, 236.8, 243.0, 154.8.
quote: repeated study after one successful recall did not produce any measurable learning a week later
limits: Single lab, one material type (word pairs), college students, one-week delay; 30 s distractor task after each study period. Per-condition N not read.
agent_relevance: Strongest founding demonstration that after first success, more recall (not more reading) is what makes memory last. A lesson recalled correctly once should still be re-retrieved, not dropped.

source: Karpicke and Blunt (2011) Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping
finding: Retrieval practice beat concept mapping (an elaborative study method), the best rival for 'it is only deeper processing'. The effect held on inference questions as well as verbatim, and students again mis-predicted which method worked.
numbers: Exp 1 collapsed over question type: retrieval 0.67 vs concept mapping 0.45, about 50% gain, d = 1.50, F(1,38) = 21.63, partial eta2 = 0.36. Exp 2: advantage over concept mapping d = 1.07 (enumeration texts) and d = 1.01 (sequence texts) on a final concept-mapping test.
limits: Science texts, college students, one-week final test; small per-experiment samples (error df 38 in Exp 1). Retrieval vs elaboration may differ with other materials.
agent_relevance: Retrieval transfers to inference questions, not only to rote recall. Relevant if stored lessons must support new problems.

source: Wing, Marsh, Cabeza (2013) Neural correlates of retrieval-based memory enhancement: an fMRI study of the testing effect
finding: When initial retrieval (rather than restudy) led to later success, anterior hippocampus, lateral temporal cortex, medial PFC and left striatum showed larger subsequent-memory effects. Hippocampus coupled more with PCC, mPFC and left ventrolateral PFC. That is encoding-like (binding, semantic elaboration) as well as retrieval-like activity.
numbers: N = 22 analysed. 192 weakly related word pairs. Final cued recall 1 day later: test 0.63 (SD 0.14) vs restudy 0.51 (SD 0.14), t(21) = 9.25, p < .0001; mean effect 0.12 (range 0.00-0.23). During practice, last-letter choice 91.3% on test vs 99.6% restudy.
limits: Shows hippocampal and mPFC engagement (fits fast consolidation) but not a hippocampal decrease. Small N.
agent_relevance: Retrieval engages the same binding and integration machinery as learning, so a retrieval step is a learning step.

source: Wiklund-Hornqvist, Stillesjo, Andersson, Jonsson, Nyberg (2021) Retrieval practice facilitates learning by strengthening processing in both the anterior and posterior hippocampus
finding: Hippocampus matters for the testing effect, with a split. Posterior hippocampus responded after even one successful retrieval and rose linearly with more. Anterior hippocampus responded only for items retrieved many times (4-6). The authors tie anterior to gist-like abstraction and posterior to episode-specific detail.
numbers: N = 50 upper-secondary students (mean age 17.9). 60 Swahili-Swedish pairs, 6 learning runs, fMRI test one week later. Behavioural testing effect: 0.53 (SE 0.03) vs 0.36 (SE 0.03), t(49) = 8.61, d = 1.22. ROI x retrievals interaction F(5,225) = 3.96, p = .002. Left-hemisphere language and semantic regions higher for retrieved items. Reversed contrast (study > retrieval) found nothing.
limits: Authors call the semantic-shift reading (via rapid consolidation, Antony 2017) speculative. Earlier fMRI testing-effect studies were mixed: some found hippocampal differences (Wing 2013, Jonker 2018), others did not (Keresztes 2013, van den Broek 2013), as cited there.
agent_relevance: Evidence of a gist route plus a detail route. Both are wanted for a lesson store: keep the specific case and the abstracted rule.

source: Ye et al. (2020) Retrieval practice facilitates memory updating by enhancing and differentiating medial prefrontal cortex representations
finding: In a 3-day A-B/A-C updating paradigm, retrieval practice of the new A-C pairs beat restudy for the new memory and cut intrusions of the old A-B memory, without suppressing A-B. MVPA showed stronger target representation in mPFC at final test. Pattern fits differentiation plus integration, not inhibition.
numbers: Exp 1 N = 19: target recall t(18) = 5.37, d = 1.30; fewer intrusions t(18) = 4.47, d = 1.04. Exp 2 N = 46: t(45) = 3.93, d = 0.57; competitor intrusions t(45) = 2.75, d = 0.36; A-B memory unchanged (t(45) = 1.43, p = .19; A-B 55.9% correct). Joint correct on both tests 24.0% vs 19.7% (d = 0.48). Exp 3 N = 28: item recall t(27) = 8.06, d = 0.50. 144 pairs.
limits: During updating, retrieval practice began near chance and cost more effort; restudy was 99.0% correct. Hippocampal decoding was at chance (35.5%). Short delay (24 h) only. Authors say mPFC role is 'probably' as in Antony 2017.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to lesson updating: when a new lesson replaces an old one, recalling the new one (not re-reading it) both strengthens it and reduces old-lesson intrusion, while keeping the old one separate.

source: Wimber, Alink, Charest, Kriegeskorte, Anderson (2015) Retrieval induces adaptive forgetting of competing memories via cortical pattern suppression
finding: Repeated retrieval of target memories suppressed cortical patterns unique to competitors, tracked with item-specific templates. The suppression linked to prefrontal engagement and predicted later forgetting. This is the weakening half of the integrate/differentiate mechanism.
numbers: N = 24. Training recall: first associates 77.1% then 86.4%; second associates 70.7%. Target category correct on 74.7% of selective retrieval trials; competitor intrusions 9.2% vs unrelated 2.3% (t23 = 6.53); intrusions fell across 4 repetitions, linear F(1,23) = 55.4. Competitor recognition 75.2% vs baseline 82.1% (t23 = 4.91, p < .001); target recognition 78.6% vs 79.7% (n.s.). Forgetting correlated with intrusions R = 0.39.
limits: A 2018 correction added a timeout-coding detail; the forgetting effect held either way (t23 = 4.91 or 3.31). Retrieval-induced forgetting is not always found; Hulbert and Norman show it can reverse with interleaved restudy.
agent_relevance: Retrieval can hurt neighbours: a cue that fires two similar lessons may weaken the loser. Design lesson keys so near-duplicates do not compete.

source: Hulbert and Norman (2015) Neural differentiation tracks improved recall of competing memories following interleaved study and retrieval practice
finding: Model-driven prediction: when restudy is interleaved with competitive retrieval, retrieval-induced forgetting can reverse into facilitation, and this goes with representational differentiation. Reduced pattern similarity in hippocampus correlated with retrieval-induced facilitation of competitors.
numbers: No numbers recorded (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only; sample size and statistics not read. Included because it ties the formal model to a boundary condition on forgetting.
agent_relevance: Interleaving retrieval with re-exposure can separate similar items rather than erase one.

source: Norman, Newman, Detre (2007) A neural network model of retrieval-induced forgetting
finding: Main formal model behind the integrate/differentiate idea. A learning algorithm uses oscillating feedback inhibition to strengthen weak parts of target memories and weaken competitors. It accounts for why retrieval gives more forgetting than re-presenting the target, and how forgetting depends on competitor and target strength.
numbers: No numbers recorded (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Model is about retrieval-induced forgetting; use for consolidation is by extension (Antony 2017).
agent_relevance: Gives a quantitative template for weakening competitors; useful if the agent ever scores lessons by strength.

source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems
finding: Founding formal theory. Neocortex learns slowly and discovers structure if items are interleaved. Hippocampus learns new items fast without disrupting that structure. Reinstatement of new memories interleaves them with old ones and integrates them over time.
numbers: Connectionist simulations; numbers not read this session.
limits: Abstract only. Original CLS says neocortical learning is slow. That is the claim that Antony 2017, Tse 2007 and Kumaran 2016 modify.
agent_relevance: CLS is the design logic for a fast episodic store plus a slow schema store; this scaffold already has a lesson store and a subgoal library.

source: Kumaran, Hassabis, McClelland (2016) What learning systems do intelligent agents need? CLS theory updated
finding: Update to CLS. Adds goal-dependent weighting of replay, generalisation through recurrent hippocampal activation, and says neocortical learning can be rapid when new information is consistent with known structure. Explicitly links to AI agent design.
numbers: No numbers (theory paper; abstract only read).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Closest bridge to AI agents: schema-consistent lessons can be stored fast; inconsistent ones need slower interleaved integration.

source: Tse et al. (2007) Schemas and memory consolidation
finding: In rats, once a flavour-place schema was built over weeks, new one-trial flavour-place pairs became hippocampus-independent very quickly. Systems consolidation can be fast when new information fits a schema.
numbers: Numbers not read this session (abstract only).
limits: Rat paired-associate task; the schema took weeks of training. Abstract only here.
agent_relevance: Basis for 'schema-consistent info integrates faster'. New lessons that fit an existing schema may need less work to stick.

source: Tse et al. (2011) Schema-dependent gene activation and memory encoding in neocortex
finding: Rat follow-up. New paired associates learned within a schema raised immediate early gene expression in prelimbic mPFC, and drug blockade of that area prevented both new learning and recall of recently and remotely consolidated pairs. Challenges the strict fast-hippocampus, slow-cortex split.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Abstract only; rodent work.
agent_relevance: Supports the mPFC prediction in Antony Box 1.

source: van Kesteren, Rijpkema, Ruiter, Fernandez (2013) Consolidation differentially modulates schema effects on memory for items and associations
finding: A schema (congruency) advantage for item recognition appeared only after consolidation (20 h and 48 h), not at 0 h. The congruency advantage for associative memory was already present at 0 h and shrank over time. So schema effects depend on memory type and delay.
numbers: N = 69 analysed (23 per group; 76 tested, 7 excluded), female students only. Item d-prime: delay x congruency F(2,66) = 5.04, p < .01; congruent better at 20 h t(22) = 2.12 and 48 h t(22) = 2.55, not at 0 h (t(22) = 1.55, n.s.). 20 fabric-object triplets, 200 motifs.
limits: Between-subject delay groups; single stimulus set; no sleep manipulation (self-reported 7.2-7.7 h). Contradicts a simple 'schema-consistent info integrates faster' claim, since an item-memory advantage needs time.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: schema fit helps some memory types early and others only after consolidation. Do not promise instant benefit for all lesson types.

source: Rowland (2014) The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect
finding: Meta-analysis supports effortful processing: initial recall tests give bigger testing benefits than recognition tests. Limited support for semantic-elaboration accounts. Suggests episodic and contextual contributions and the bifurcation model.
numbers: Effect-size figures not read this session (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only, so no g value recorded here. Cited by Antony 2017 as the evidence base for the testing effect.
agent_relevance: Recall-type retrieval (produce the answer) beats recognition-type (choose it); a scaffold should force production of the lesson, not a yes/no check.

source: Pyc and Rawson (2010) Why testing improves memory: mediator effectiveness hypothesis
finding: Competing non-consolidation account: practice tests with restudy lead learners to generate mediators (cue-to-target links) that are more retrievable and more likely to elicit the target at final test.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Abstract only. A behavioural account that needs no hippocampal story.
agent_relevance: A lesson stored with its own cue-to-answer link (a mediator) is the practical version.

source: Rickard and Pan (2018) A dual memory theory of the testing effect
finding: Competing quantitative theory: separate memories form from study and test events. With no free parameters, the simplest-case model predicts test-condition accuracy and testing-effect size across 10 experiments, including feedback, retention interval and effect of prior learning method.
numbers: 10 experiments from the authors' lab; parameter-free predictions. No effect sizes read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Rival to the consolidation account; does not use hippocampal-neocortical transfer.
agent_relevance: Two independent traces (study trace plus test trace) can explain the effect without consolidation.

source: Rickard (2020) Extension of the dual-memory model to distributions and individual differences; and a 2022 paper, Prior episodic learning and the efficacy of retrieval practice
finding: Distribution predictions of the dual-memory model hold across 509 subjects and 1-7 day delays. A 2022 three-experiment test found the testing advantage over restudy is independent of the amount of prior study (1 to 8 repetitions).
numbers: 509 subjects pooled; 3 experiments in 2022 (abstract only; no further numbers).
limits: Abstract only. The 2022 result is a quiet test of Antony 2017: a consolidation-by-schema account might predict bigger gains with more prior learning, and none was found.
agent_relevance: The testing benefit does not seem to depend on how well the item was first learned; do not wait for deep prior knowledge before retrieving.

source: Bauml, Holterman, Abel (2014) Sleep can reduce the testing effect
finding: 5 experiments: testing effect after 12 h wake, but reduced or eliminated after sleep, since sleep helped restudied items and left retrieved items unchanged. Authors read it with the bifurcation model: retrieved items are already above threshold.
numbers: 5 experiments, 12-h delay; effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Used by Antony 2017 as support but explained differently by the original authors.
agent_relevance: Consolidation-like benefit for retrieved items is saturated; extra re-checks add less for items already retrieved.

source: Bauml and colleagues (2019) Sleep reduces the testing effect - but not after corrective feedback and prolonged retention interval
finding: Boundary conditions on the sleep result. With corrective feedback, sleep helped retrieval-practised items too. At 24 h and 7 days, no lasting sleep benefit for either restudied or retrieved items. So the sleep-reduces-testing-effect pattern is narrow.
numbers: 4 experiments; 12 h (Exp 1a, 1b), 24 h and 7 days (Exp 2a, 2b). No effect sizes read.
limits: Abstract only. Weakens the sleep parallel offered in Antony 2017.
agent_relevance: Feedback matters; a retrieval step that shows the right answer afterward behaves differently from one that does not.

source: Potts and Shanks (2012) Can testing immunize memories against interference?
finding: Direct test of reconsolidation vs consolidation view. A reminder test of List 1 before learning List 2 did not impair List 1 but enhanced it and immunised it against List 2 interference. This is the opposite of what reconsolidation (destabilisation) would predict.
numbers: 20 English-Swahili pairs (List 1) and 20 English-Finnish pairs (List 2), 4 groups, 3 days; no further numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Supports retrieval as strengthening, against retrieval as destabilising.
agent_relevance: Retrieving an old lesson before adding a new, overlapping lesson protects the old one.

source: Hardwicke, Taqi, Shanks (2016) Postretrieval new learning does not reliably induce human memory updating via reconsolidation
finding: Failed replication of the motor-sequence reconsolidation result of Walker et al. (2003). No impairment effect in four direct replications; in three conceptual replications retrieval helped preserve the sequence instead of destabilising it.
numbers: 4 direct replications n = 64 total; 3 conceptual replications n = 48.
limits: Abstract only. Reconsolidation in humans is contested; the consolidation-through-retrieval view and the reconsolidation view make opposite predictions about post-retrieval vulnerability.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that recalling a lesson makes it fragile. Evidence points the other way in humans.

source: Replication on retrieval context (2019) Exploring the role of context on the existing evidence for reconsolidation of episodic memory
finding: Tested retrieval context as a rival to Hupbach et al. (2007). The intrusion effect (List 2 items in List 1 recall after a reminder) occurred regardless of retrieval context and depended on reactivation. This supports the original effect.
numbers: Two experiments; no counts read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Shows the reconsolidation-style intrusion effect holds in at least one lab, so the field is split rather than settled.
agent_relevance: A reminder cue can pull in related new material (integration), which is also the prediction of Antony 2017.

source: Sharon, Moscovitch, Gilboa (2011) Rapid neocortical acquisition of long-term arbitrary associations independent of the hippocampus; with Himmer et al. (2017) on fast mapping and sleep
finding: Four amnesic patients learned new word-picture links by fast mapping normally and kept them after a week, when they were at chance on the standard task. In healthy adults, fast-mapped associations did not gain from sleep while explicitly learned ones did. Both support rapid cortical embedding when prior knowledge is used.
numbers: 4 hippocampal amnesic patients, 2 left temporal-pole patients; healthy-adult sleep result from Himmer 2017 (no numbers read).
limits: Abstracts only; small patient N. Fast mapping is a different paradigm from retrieval; the link is by analogy in Antony 2017.
agent_relevance: Using prior knowledge to infer a new item (rather than rote copying) may bypass the slow stage.

source: Lehmann et al. (2009) Making context memories independent of the hippocampus
finding: In rodents, repeated learning sessions created context memories that survived later hippocampal damage even when recent. Evidence that repeated reactivation can make memories hippocampus-independent without a long delay.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only; rodent context learning, not retrieval vs restudy.
agent_relevance: Repetition across sessions can matter, not only within one.

source: Roediger and Butler (2011) The critical role of retrieval practice in long-term retention
finding: Review. Retrieval practice often yields large long-term gains over repeated study, helps even without feedback (feedback adds more), and promotes knowledge that can be retrieved flexibly and transferred. Calls retrieval a consolidation process.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only here. The Chinese 2024 article named in the subfield row was not located in this session.
agent_relevance: Framing source for the phrase retrieval as consolidation.
